clinical_category: Epileptic seizure classification - current focal and generalized terminology
blueprint_topic: Recognition and communication of seizure type using current clinical classification
stem: A nurse reviews seizure documentation for a client with epilepsy. Which statement is consistent with the current 2025 ILAE classification of epileptic seizures?

options.A: Focal and generalized remain distinct main seizure classes, alongside unknown whether focal or generalized and unclassified
options.B: A seizure can be classified as generalized only when complete loss of consciousness is documented
options.C: Motor versus non-motor manifestations remain the primary required division used by the updated classification
options.D: Seizure classification should rely only on the first observed sign and should not describe the later sequence of manifestations

rationale: A is correct. The 2025 International League Against Epilepsy classification retains four main seizure classes: Focal, Generalized, Unknown whether focal or generalized, and Unclassified. The update also distinguishes classifiers from descriptors, replaces 'awareness' with 'consciousness' as a classifier, replaces the motor versus non-motor dichotomy with observable versus non-observable manifestations, and emphasizes describing the chronological sequence of seizure signs and symptoms rather than relying only on the first sign. B incorrectly makes loss of consciousness a universal definition of generalized seizures. C and D directly contradict the 2025 changes. The original item was rebuilt because its statement that generalized seizures are characterized by bilateral involvement 'typically with loss of consciousness' was an oversimplification of the current classification framework.
educational_objective: Use the current ILAE seizure-classification framework accurately: distinguish focal, generalized, unknown, and unclassified seizure classes and avoid defining generalized seizures solely by loss of consciousness or by the first observed manifestation.
source_document_title: Updated classification of epileptic seizures: Position paper of the International League Against Epilepsy
source_version_date: First published 2025-04-23; listed by ILAE as the current updated seizure classification and accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: ILAE 'Updated classification of epileptic seizures (2025)' → main classification and 'Six key changes': four main seizure classes are Focal, Generalized, Unknown whether focal or generalized, and Unclassified; 'onset' is removed from the main class names; consciousness replaces awareness as a classifier; motor/non-motor is replaced by observable/non-observable manifestations; seizure description follows the chronological sequence rather than relying solely on the first sign.
source_claim_supported: The current ILAE 2025 position paper directly supports the four main seizure classes and the classification changes used to distinguish the correct answer from each distractor.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation client-needs subcategory (11–17% of items); this item tests recognition and communication of an acute/chronic neurologic alteration using current clinical terminology.
correction_summary: Total currentness rebuild. The original secondary Epilepsy Foundation item used an oversimplified generalized-versus-focal distinction and linked generalized seizures too closely to loss of consciousness. The final item uses the current 2025 ILAE classification and tests the exact main seizure classes and updated classifier/descriptor framework without unsupported neuroanatomic or consciousness generalizations.
audit_findings: The original secondary source did not reflect the most current ILAE seizure-classification framework.
ILAE's current 2025 position paper retains Focal and Generalized as separate main seizure classes alongside Unknown and Unclassified.
The final item removes the oversimplified implication that loss of consciousness defines generalized seizures.
Each distractor is directly excluded by one of the explicit 2025 classification changes, reducing ambiguity and avoiding fabricated pathophysiology.
Independent adversarial second pass found one uniquely correct answer, no second defensible option, no cueing, no unsupported numerical or neuroanatomic precision, and no unresolved conflict.
